title: Visualization of the Primo Vascular System,a Putative Cancer Metastasis Thread Afloat in a Lymph Duct
protocol: Anesthetize the rat with an intramuscular injection of zolatil and xylazine using a sterile hypodermic syringe.
Remove hair from the abdominal and flank/hip areas using a Pet Specialty cordless trimmer shaver.
Remove loose hair from the area with alcohol swabs and tape.
Tape the rat's feet to the operating surgical board, positioning its head away from the operator.
Cover the rat’s eyes with gauze before surgery for protection from light exposure.
Position fiber optic illuminators for optimum illumination.
Adjust the stereomicroscope and monitoring system for optimal observation.
Monitor the rat continually during the procedure via toe pinch and examination of respiratory rate.
Keep exposed tissue wet with equilibrated warmed PBS solution throughout the surgical procedure.
Place the rat on a clear surgical board in a supine frog-leg position, attaching each footpad to the board.
Check the body temperature of the rat during the procedure.
Make a 2-cm skin midline incision up and down from the navel along the ventral surface of the abdominal cavity.
Retract the skin towards the rat's spinal column.
Pin the retracted skin to the surgery board.
Place rolled sheets of clean gauze underneath the skin for easier IN location.
Locate the inguinal lymph node (IN) near the superficial epigastric vein bifurcation.
Pull the rat’s lower limb on the finding side towards your body if necessary to extend its position and aid in locating the IN.
Remove the thin layer of connective tissue overlaying the area around the IN.
Clear the adipose tissue overlaying and surrounding the IN until the micro-vascular bed is exposed.
Expose the IN for injection.
Hold the tip of the IN and slightly lift it up towards your body with smooth tip forceps.
Inject about 0.2~0.4 ml of prepared 0.2% Alcian blue dye into the node at a slow rate using a specially designed syringe.
Choose the uppermost IN among the group for injection to reach axillary nodes.
If injecting middle or undermost INs, staining dye will travel towards the abdominal area through lymph vessels.
Inject AB into the nodes on each side of the skin at a rate not exceeding 0.03 mL/4 min.
Wait for approximately 3-5 minutes until the injection site is stabilized.
Gently pull out the needle after completing the injection.
Check the rat’s respiratory rate to ensure spontaneous pumping.
Return the skin to its original position to maintain body warmth.
Tie a string in the upper chest to stop lymph flow from the IN to the axillary node for 30 minutes.
Release the tie after 30 minutes to allow proper lymph fluid flow.
Wash out residual AB staining in the lymph ducts using natural lymphatic flow, which takes about one and half hours.
Make the lymph flow fast during the washing period.
Incise the skin starting from the endpoint of the first cutting near the navel about 4 cm towards the cranium.
Turn the skin towards the spinal column and pin it to a surgical board for clear observation of the lymph ducts.
Trace lymph ducts along the superior epigastric vein.
Identify the axillary node due to the blue color of the AB in the lymph ducts from the IN.
Locate brachial and retoscapular lymph nodes near the angle of the scapula.
Use a stereomicroscope to examine along the lymph ducts in the skin.
Observe freely-floating, thin, blue PVS lines inside washed lymph vessels.
Look for irregularly located primo nodes (PNs) that appear as thicker oval-shaped blobs.
Attempt to observe numerous specimens of PVS network structures with branches.
Carefully observe PV passing through lymph valves.
Observe PVs in efferent ducts flowing from the interstitial node (IN).
Observe PVs in afferent ducts flowing to the axillary node (AN).
Shake the lymph duct gently but briskly to observe the movement of the PVS.
Ensure the blue threadlike structure remains unbroken during shaking.
Distinguish aggregates of dye from the continuous, undulating PVS.
Observe that the thickness of the PV is uniform and measures about 20-30 μm.
If a PV is cut accidentally, it will roll up due to elasticity and can be pulled out without breaking.
Cut out the whole lymph nodes and ducts containing the PVS from the skin under a stereomicroscope.
Carefully incise the lymph vessel along its wall using microscissors.
Hold both sides of the split lymph vessel with sharp-ended curved forceps and tear it apart towards the direction of the axillary node.
Gently pull out an appropriate length of PVS specimen toward your body, being careful not to damage it.
Fix the whole isolated samples with either 4% PFA solution or 10% NBF solution for a day or two.
Wash the fixed sample with 1x PBS solution three times.
Prepare a glass slide with 1 drop of 1x PBS solution to protect the sample from drying during the procedure.
Put the fixed whole sample on a slide.
Use two 31G insulin syringe needle tips to cut and tear the lymph duct to extract the PVS specimen.
Cut one end of the lymph vessel obliquely at 45° from the surface of skin.
Tear the lower end of a harvested lymph vessel with sharp-end forceps and expose the end part of the PVS in it.
Pull the PV gently out.
Gently wash the PVS specimen in a drop of 1x PBS solution.
Place the washed PVS on a clean glass slide.
Flatten the tissue slightly under a stereomicroscope.
Check the bundle structure of the PV using a phase contrast microscope.
Check the alignment of rod-shaped nuclei in endothelial cells lining the sub-vessel using DAPI staining.
Mix Prolong Gold Antifade reagent thoroughly with DAPI and stain the specimen for 10 minutes.
Drain excess solution from the slide after DAPI staining.
Apply two separate drops of Gel Mount – DAPI on the sections.
Lower the cover slip onto the sections.
Allow the slide to stay in darkness for a few minutes.
Seal the cover slip with transparent manicure.
Stain the specimen with 6.6-μM Phalloidin for 20 minutes.
Wash the specimen with PBS three times after Phalloidin staining.
Examine the specimens using fluorescence phase contrast microscopy to observe f-actins and rod-shaped nuclei.
Observe the specimens with a confocal laser scanning microscope to examine f-actins and rod-shaped nuclei.
